extracted.intended_audience: students, policymakers, and readers of political economy interested in trade policy and the historical corn laws
extracted.subtask_short: evaluating trade policy and corn laws
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts principles for assessing laws and policies affecting the corn/grain trade, import/export duties, bounties, carrying trade, and commercial treaties, with historical examples and normative recommendations. Useful for analyzing the effects of trade regulation on domestic supply, tillage, and national welfare.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom and protection of the inland corn trade
rubrics_metrics.description: It is from [the 15th of Charles II. c. 7] that the inland corn trade has derived all the liberty and protection which it has ever yet enjoyed; and both the supply of the home market and the interest of tillage are much more effectually promoted by the inland, than either by the importation or exportation trade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promote liberty and protection for inland dealers because the inland trade is the most important for supplying the home market and encouraging tillage; laws that secure freedom for inland commerce help keep corn plentiful domestically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative importance of inland trade versus foreign trade for the home market
rubrics_metrics.description: The proportion of the average quantity of all sorts of grain imported into Great Britain to that of all sorts of grain consumed ... does not exceed that of one to five hundred and seventy. ... The average quantity of all sorts of grain exported ... does not exceed the one-and-thirtieth part of the annual produce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these magnitudes (inland trade far outweighs importation; importance to tillage much greater than exportation) as evidence when evaluating whether policy should prioritize inland-trade freedoms over import/export restrictions, while noting the author's caveat that 'I have no great faith in political arithmetic.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Benefits of merchant-importers (importation for home consumption)
rubrics_metrics.description: The trade of the merchant-importer of foreign corn for home consumption evidently contributes to the immediate supply of the home market, and must so far be immediately beneficial to the great body of the people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that importation lowers the money price of corn without reducing its real value, can raise the real value of silver, enlarge markets, and encourage industry; therefore, freer importation should not be presumed to discourage domestic cultivation on real-value grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impropriety of permanent restraints on importation (use temporary measures only in necessity)
rubrics_metrics.description: The necessity of these temporary statutes sufficiently demonstrates the impropriety of this general one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permanent high duties or prohibitions on importation are typically harmful; suspension by temporary statutes during scarcity shows such general restraints are improper. Policy should avoid constant import restrictions and reserve restrictive measures for exceptional, urgent circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Export freedom encourages production; prohibitions limit cultivation
rubrics_metrics.description: The prohibition of exportation limits the improvement and cultivation of the country to what the supply of its own inhabitants require. The freedom of exportation enables it to extend cultivation for the supply of foreign nations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allowing exportation typically incentivizes growers to produce more (because they can sell abroad), so routine prohibitions on exportation reduce production and national improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risks from merchant-exporters during domestic dearth — restrict exportation only in urgent necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: If, while his own country labours under a dearth, a neighbouring country should be afflicted with a famine, it might be [the merchant-exporter's] interest to carry corn to the latter country, in such quantities as might very much aggravate the calamities of the dearth. ... To hinder, besides, the farmer from sending his goods at all times to the best market, is evidently to sacrifice the ordinary laws of justice to an idea of public utility, ... which ought to be exercised only, which can be pardoned only, in cases of the most urgent necessity. The price at which exportation of corn is prohibited, if it is ever to be prohibited, ought always to be a very high price.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary that exporters can aggravate domestic scarcity; therefore, any prohibition on exportation should be reserved for the most urgent necessities and be triggered only at very high price thresholds to avoid unjustly denying sellers access to the best market.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bounties on export are improper and distortionary
rubrics_metrics.description: If bounties are as improper as I have endeavoured to prove them to be, the sooner they cease, and the lower they are, so much the better. ... The bounty, which was given in order to force [exportation], is withdrawn [at a price] — the bounty ought certainly either to have been withdrawn at a much lower price, or exportation ought to have been allowed at a much higher.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid or minimize export bounties because they artificially encourage exportation, raise domestic prices, and can pervert the institution's aims. If used, design cessation thresholds carefully to avoid inconsistency with export prohibition rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Carrying trade (import to re-export) supports home supply
rubrics_metrics.description: The trade of the merchant-carrier, or of the importer of foreign corn, in order to export it again, contributes to the plentiful supply of the home market. ... he will generally be willing to do so, and even for a good deal less money than he might expect in a foreign market; because he saves in this manner the expense of loading and unloading, of freight and insurance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Facilitate the carrying trade (including duty-free re-export when properly warehoused) because it supplies the home market at lower prices and stabilizes supply; high import duties and lack of warehouse facilities effectively prohibit this beneficial trade.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treaties of commerce grant monopolies and can disadvantage domestic producers
rubrics_metrics.description: When a nation binds itself by treaty, either to permit the entry of certain goods from one foreign country which it prohibits from all others, or to exempt the goods of one country from duties to which it subjects those of all others, the country, or at least the merchants and manufacturers of the country, whose commerce is so favoured, must necessarily derive great advantage from the treaty. ... Such treaties ... are necessarily disadvantageous to those of the favouring country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate commercial treaties by weighing the advantage to favored foreign merchants (a de facto monopoly in your market) against the disadvantage to domestic merchants and the likely diminution of the exchangeable value of the nation's annual produce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer direct consumption trade to round-about trade mediated by precious metals
rubrics_metrics.description: A direct foreign trade of consumption is always more advantageous than a round-about one; and to bring the same value of foreign goods to the home market requires a much smaller capital in the one way than in the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor policies and trade patterns that import consumable goods directly rather than purchasing gold/silver to buy them indirectly, because direct trade requires less capital and is more efficient, even though gold and silver are convenient for round-about trades.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not overvalue the balance-of-trade notion (Portugal trade example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Almost all our gold, it is said, comes from Portugal. ... The more gold we import from one country, the less we must necessarily import from all others. ... The effectual demand for gold ... is limited to a certain quantity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be skeptical of claims that a particular trade (e.g., Portugal trade) is indispensable because of gold inflows; balance-of-trade arguments that focus on accumulating gold from one partner are often mistaken about net national benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Security of property and general liberty are primary drivers of national prosperity
rubrics_metrics.description: That security which the laws in Great Britain give to every man, that he shall enjoy the fruits of his own labour, is alone sufficient to make any country flourish ... The natural effort of every individual to better his own condition, when suffered to exert itself with freedom and security, is so powerful a principle ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize legal security and individual liberty over intricate commercial regulations: secure property rights and freedom of industry are more decisive for national wealth than many trade laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy design should consider state size and ease of internal communication
rubrics_metrics.description: The unlimited freedom of exportation, however, would be much less dangerous in great states, in which the growth being much greater, the supply could seldom be much affected by any quantity of corn that was likely to be exported. In a Swiss canton ... it may, perhaps, sometimes be necessary to restrain the exportation of corn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor export/import freedoms to the country's geographic size and the ease of inter-regional communication: large states can safely allow more freedom, while very small or poorly connected states may need occasional restraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislation is often shaped by popular prejudice; strive for reasonable systems despite pressures
rubrics_metrics.description: The laws concerning corn may everywhere be compared to the laws concerning religion. The people feel themselves so much interested ... that government must yield to their prejudices, and, in order to preserve the public tranquillity, establish that system which they approve of.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that public sentiment can force governments into suboptimal laws; policymakers should be aware of this tendency and work to establish more reasonable systems while managing public tranquility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design consistency between bounties and export prohibitions
rubrics_metrics.description: There seems to be an impropriety, besides, in prohibiting exportation altogether at those precise prices at which that bounty, which was given in order to force it, is withdrawn. The bounty ought certainly either to have been withdrawn at a much lower price, or exportation ought to have been allowed at a much higher.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure that the thresholds and mechanisms for granting/withdrawing bounties are consistent with export-prohibition rules to avoid perverse incentives and policy contradictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use warehousing and procedural facilitation to enable duty-free import-for-reexport
rubrics_metrics.description: The same statute permits, at the lowest prices, the importation of corn in order to be exported again, duty free, provided it is in the mean time lodged in a warehouse under the joint locks of the king and the importer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement practical measures (e.g., bonded warehouses with appropriate oversight) to allow importation for re-export without duties in select ports, facilitating carrying trade; be mindful of port and infrastructure limitations.
